claim: The umbilical artery lumen closes rapidly at birth, preventing neonatal blood loss.
source: The umbilical artery lumen closes rapidly at birth, preventing neonatal blood loss, whereas the umbilical vein remains patent longer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The umbilical vein remains patent longer than the umbilical artery at birth.
source: The umbilical artery lumen closes rapidly at birth, preventing neonatal blood loss, whereas the umbilical vein remains patent longer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The umbilical artery has an inner layer enriched in the hydrated proteoglycan aggrecan.
source: The umbilical artery, but not the vein, has an inner layer enriched in the hydrated proteoglycan aggrecan, external to which lie contraction-primed smooth muscle cells (SMC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining and histological data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Contraction-primed smooth muscle cells lie external to the aggrecan-rich inner layer in the umbilical artery.
source: The umbilical artery, but not the vein, has an inner layer enriched in the hydrated proteoglycan aggrecan, external to which lie contraction-primed smooth muscle cells (SMC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pMLC staining data shown in Figure 7.

claim: SMC contraction drives inner layer buckling and centripetal displacement to occlude the arterial lumen at birth.
source: At birth, SMC contraction drives inner layer buckling and centripetal displacement to occlude the arterial lumen, a mechanism revealed by biomechanical observations and confirmed by computational analyses.
evidence: This mechanism is described in the abstract and supported by biomechanical testing (Figure 7c) and computational modeling (Figure 7d-e).

claim: Vascular dimorphism arises from spatially regulated proteoglycan expression and breakdown.
source: This vascular dimorphism arises from spatially regulated proteoglycan expression and breakdown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA in situ hybridization data (Figures 1f, 2a) and immunostaining for proteoglycan cleavage products (Figure 2b).

claim: Mice lacking aggrecan demonstrate the role of aggrecan in umbilical vascular dimorphism.
source: Mice lacking aggrecan or the metalloprotease ADAMTS1, which degrades proteoglycans, demonstrate their opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism, including effects on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from Acan-/- mice showing altered vessel morphology and SMC markers (Figures 4, 5).

claim: Mice lacking ADAMTS1 demonstrate the role of ADAMTS1 in umbilical vascular dimorphism.
source: Mice lacking aggrecan or the metalloprotease ADAMTS1, which degrades proteoglycans, demonstrate their opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism, including effects on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from Adamts1-/- mice showing altered vessel morphology and proteoglycan accumulation (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claim: ADAMTS1 degrades proteoglycans.
source: Mice lacking aggrecan or the metalloprotease ADAMTS1, which degrades proteoglycans, demonstrate their opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism, including effects on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about ADAMTS1 function, also supported by neo-epitope staining (Figure 2b).

claim: Aggrecan and ADAMTS1 have opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism.
source: Mice lacking aggrecan or the metalloprotease ADAMTS1, which degrades proteoglycans, demonstrate their opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism, including effects on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by contrasting phenotypes in Acan-/- and Adamts1-/- mice (Figures 4-6).

claim: Aggrecan and ADAMTS1 affect SMC differentiation in umbilical vessels.
source: Mice lacking aggrecan or the metalloprotease ADAMTS1, which degrades proteoglycans, demonstrate their opposing roles in umbilical vascular dimorphism, including effects on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by altered SMC marker expression in mutant mice (Figure 5).

claim: Umbilical vessel dimorphism is conserved in mammals.
source: Umbilical vessel dimorphism is conserved in mammals, suggesting that differential proteoglycan dynamics and inner layer buckling were positively selected during evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis of umbilical cords from nine large mammalian species (Figure 3).

claim: Differential proteoglycan dynamics and inner layer buckling were positively selected during evolution.
source: Umbilical vessel dimorphism is conserved in mammals, suggesting that differential proteoglycan dynamics and inner layer buckling were positively selected during evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the mechanism across multiple mammalian species.

claim: The umbilical cord typically contains two arteries and one vein in humans.
source: The umbilical cord, typically containing two arteries and one vein in humans, is a crucial fetal structure in placental mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placental vascular bed.
source: Umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placental vascular bed, whereas the umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established physiological knowledge.

claim: The umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus.
source: Umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placental vascular bed, whereas the umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established physiological knowledge.

claim: Neonatal respiration at birth renders the maternal oxygen supply redundant.
source: Neonatal respiration at birth renders the maternal oxygen supply redundant.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established physiological knowledge.

claim: Umbilical arteries commence closure rapidly after delivery of the newborn.
source: Umbilical arteries commence closure rapidly after delivery of the newborn whereas the veins remain open longer.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by histological observations (Figure 1b).

claim: The cord is routinely clamped following delivery and divided between the clamps in modern obstetric practice.
source: The cord is routinely clamped following delivery and divided between the clamps in modern obstetric practice.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established clinical practice.

claim: Timing of cord clamping after birth is extensively debated.
source: Timing of cord clamping after birth, whether early or late, is extensively debated (Niermeyer, 2015; Tarnow-Mordi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: A recent recommendation suggested clamping no earlier than 30–60 s after birth to facilitate the placental transfusion.
source: A recent recommendation suggested clamping no earlier than 30–60 s after birth to facilitate the placental transfusion (TACoOaG, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cord clamping appears to be a modern practice.
source: Although the necessity of clamping is rarely questioned, it appears to be a modern practice (Downey and Bewley, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Cord clamping is rarely practiced in domesticated animals and certainly not in wild animals.
source: Cord clamping is rarely practiced in domesticated animals and certainly not in wild animals, yet all current mammalian species have survived evolutionarily.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on general knowledge of animal husbandry and wildlife.

claim: All current mammalian species have survived evolutionarily without cord clamping.
source: Cord clamping is rarely practiced in domesticated animals and certainly not in wild animals, yet all current mammalian species have survived evolutionarily.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Umbilical arteries have a bilaminar structure.
source: Prior histological work revealed that umbilical arteries have a bilaminar structure (Meyer et al., 1978) but lack elastic lamellae, which endow large arteries with resilience during cyclic loading (Wagenseil and Mecham, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work, as well as confirmed by the current study's data (Figure 1).

claim: Umbilical arteries lack elastic lamellae.
source: Prior histological work revealed that umbilical arteries have a bilaminar structure (Meyer et al., 1978) but lack elastic lamellae, which endow large arteries with resilience during cyclic loading (Wagenseil and Mecham, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Elastic lamellae endow large arteries with resilience during cyclic loading.
source: Prior histological work revealed that umbilical arteries have a bilaminar structure (Meyer et al., 1978) but lack elastic lamellae, which endow large arteries with resilience during cyclic loading (Wagenseil and Mecham, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying the bilayered structure of umbilical arteries and its relationship to arterial occlusion remains obscure.
source: However, the molecular mechanism underlying the bilayered structure and its relationship to arterial occlusion remains obscure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The umbilical artery has a much thicker tunica media than the vein.
source: Three-dimensional imaging of term human umbilical cords, using synchrotron-based phase contrast micro-CT with effective pixel size 1.63 × 1.63 μm2 (Norvik et al., 2020) and histology, identified a much thicker tunica media (TM) in the umbilical artery than in the vein, with a visibly different structure (Figure 1a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c, Figure 1—videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by synchrotron imaging and histology shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most umbilical arteries were occluded at birth independent of delivery method or cord region analyzed.
source: Most umbilical arteries were occluded at birth independent of delivery method or cord region analyzed, whereas umbilical veins remained patent (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Umbilical veins remained patent at birth.
source: Most umbilical arteries were occluded at birth independent of delivery method or cord region analyzed, whereas umbilical veins remained patent (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Smooth muscle cell markers showed similar staining intensities within inner and outer TM of the umbilical arteries and TM of the vein.
source: Smooth muscle cell (SMC) markers showed similar staining intensities within inner and outer TM of the umbilical arteries and TM of the vein with alternating layers of longitudinal and circumferentially oriented SMCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Umbilical arteries and veins have alternating layers of longitudinal and circumferentially oriented SMCs.
source: Smooth muscle cell (SMC) markers showed similar staining intensities within inner and outer TM of the umbilical arteries and TM of the vein with alternating layers of longitudinal and circumferentially oriented SMCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: The veins showed fewer layers of SMCs compared to the arteries.
source: The veins showed fewer layers of SMCs compared to the arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Alcian blue intensely stained the inner layer of the bilayered arterial TM.
source: Alcian blue, which binds sulfated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), intensely stained the inner layer of the bilayered arterial TM but only the innermost three to four cell layers of the venous TM (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological staining shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Alcian blue binds sulfated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs).
source: Alcian blue, which binds sulfated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), intensely stained the inner layer of the bilayered arterial TM but only the innermost three to four cell layers of the venous TM (Figure 1c).

claim: Alcian blue stained only the innermost three to four cell layers of the venous TM.
source: Alcian blue, which binds sulfated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), intensely stained the inner layer of the bilayered arterial TM but only the innermost three to four cell layers of the venous TM (Figure 1c).

claim: SMCs in the GAG-rich region of the arteries were radially oriented and round.
source: SMCs in this GAG-rich region of the arteries were radially oriented and round, with nuclear-localized Sox9, a chondrogenic factor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e; Ng et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: SMCs in the GAG-rich region of the arteries have nuclear-localized Sox9.
source: SMCs in this GAG-rich region of the arteries were radially oriented and round, with nuclear-localized Sox9, a chondrogenic factor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e; Ng et al., 1997).

claim: Sox9 is a chondrogenic factor.

claim: The distribution of chondroitin sulfate coincided with Alcian blue staining in umbilical arteries.
source: The distribution of chondroitin sulfate (CS) coincided with Alcian blue staining (Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), whereas heparan sulfate was more abundant in the outer arterial TM (Figure 1d), suggesting that the inner TM was enriched in CS-proteoglycans (CSPGs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: Heparan sulfate was more abundant in the outer arterial TM.
source: The distribution of chondroitin sulfate (CS) coincided with Alcian blue staining (Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), whereas heparan sulfate was more abundant in the outer arterial TM (Figure 1d), suggesting that the inner TM was enriched in CS-proteoglycans (CSPGs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The inner TM of umbilical arteries was enriched in CS-proteoglycans (CSPGs).
source: The distribution of chondroitin sulfate (CS) coincided with Alcian blue staining (Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), whereas heparan sulfate was more abundant in the outer arterial TM (Figure 1d), suggesting that the inner TM was enriched in CS-proteoglycans (CSPGs).

claim: RNA microarray data from matched human umbilical arteries and veins showed arterial prevalence of mRNAs for ACAN and VCAN.

claim: ACAN encodes aggrecan.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is established knowledge.

claim: VCAN encodes versican.
source: RNA microarray data from matched human umbilical arteries and veins showed, among many differentially expressed genes (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Sup. array data-1), arterial prevalence of mRNAs for ACAN and VCAN encoding CSPGs bearing the most CS-chains, aggrecan and versican, respectively (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is established knowledge.

claim: Aggrecan and versican are CSPGs bearing the most CS-chains.
source: RNA microarray data from matched human umbilical arteries and veins showed, among many differentially expressed genes (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Sup. array data-1), arterial prevalence of mRNAs for ACAN and VCAN encoding CSPGs bearing the most CS-chains, aggrecan and versican, respectively (Figure 1e).

claim: Microarray analysis of the inner versus outer arterial TM identified stronger ACAN and VCAN expression in the inner TM.
source: Microarray analysis of the inner versus outer arterial TM identified stronger ACAN and VCAN expression in the inner TM, among other differences (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Sup. array data-2).

source: RNA in situ hybridization (RNA-ISH) localized strong ACAN and VCAN expression in inner arterial TM SMC, and immunostaining showed versican and aggrecan core proteins in a similar distribution as alcian blue and anti-CS staining (Figure 1c,d,f).

claim: Versican and aggrecan core proteins showed similar distribution as alcian blue and anti-CS staining.
source: RNA in situ hybridization (RNA-ISH) localized strong ACAN and VCAN expression in inner arterial TM SMC, and immunostaining showed versican and aggrecan core proteins in a similar distribution as alcian blue and anti-CS staining (Figure 1c,d,f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1c,d,f.

claim: Versican is a well-characterized vascular component.
source: Versican is a well-characterized vascular component (Wight and Merrilees, 2004), and aggrecan, which is known as a cartilage and neural proteoglycan (Lauing et al., 2014; Schwartz and Domowicz, 2014), is emerging as a significant CSPG in vascular disease (reviewed in Koch et al., 2020).

claim: Aggrecan is known as a cartilage and neural proteoglycan.
source: Versican is a well-characterized vascular component (Wight and Merrilees, 2004), and aggrecan, which is known as a cartilage and neural proteoglycan (Lauing et al., 2014; Schwartz and Domowicz, 2014), is emerging as a significant CSPG in vascular disease (reviewed in Koch et al., 2020).

claim: Aggrecan is emerging as a significant CSPG in vascular disease.

claim: Aggrecan and versican are proteolytically cleaved by ADAMTS1, 4, 5, and 9.
source: Aggrecan and versican are proteolytically cleaved by ADAMTS1, 4, 5, and 9 (Dancevic et al., 2016).

source: ADAMTS1 and ADAMTS4 mRNAs had higher levels in the venous wall in microarrays (Figure 1e, Sup. Array data-1), and RNA-ISH demonstrated stronger expression of ADAMTS1, ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, and ADAMTS9 in the veins (Figure 2a).

claim: RNA-ISH demonstrated stronger expression of ADAMTS1, ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, and ADAMTS9 in the veins.
source: ADAMTS1 and ADAMTS4 mRNAs had higher levels in the venous wall in microarrays (Figure 1e, Sup. Array data-1), and RNA-ISH demonstrated stronger expression of ADAMTS1, ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, and ADAMTS9 in the veins (Figure 2a).

claim: ADAMTS1 was the most strongly expressed ADAMTS protease in umbilical vessels.
source: ADAMTS1 was the most strongly expressed, localizing to venous endothelium and TM, with stronger umbilical artery expression seen in the outer than inner TM (Figure 2a).

claim: ADAMTS1 localizes to venous endothelium and TM.
source: ADAMTS1 was the most strongly expressed, localizing to venous endothelium and TM, with stronger umbilical artery expression seen in the outer than inner TM (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: ADAMTS1 showed stronger expression in the outer than inner TM of umbilical arteries.
source: ADAMTS1 was the most strongly expressed, localizing to venous endothelium and TM, with stronger umbilical artery expression seen in the outer than inner TM (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: ADAMTS9 was similarly expressed as ADAMTS1 in umbilical vessels.
source: ADAMTS9 was similarly expressed as ADAMTS1, whereas ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5 mRNAs were restricted to umbilical vein endothelium and some venous SMC (Figure 2a).

claim: ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5 mRNAs were restricted to umbilical vein endothelium and some venous SMC.
source: ADAMTS9 was similarly expressed as ADAMTS1, whereas ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5 mRNAs were restricted to umbilical vein endothelium and some venous SMC (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Neo-epitope antibodies detecting ADAMTS-cleaved aggrecan and versican showed strong staining throughout the venous TM and in the outer arterial TM, but not the inner arterial TM.
source: Neo-epitope antibodies detecting ADAMTS-cleaved aggrecan and versican (anti-NITEGE and anti-DPEAAE, respectively) (Lark et al., 1995; Sandy et al., 1992; Sandy et al., 2001) showed strong staining throughout the venous TM and in the outer arterial TM, but not the inner arterial TM (Figure 2b).

claim: Proteoglycan accumulation in the inner TM of the umbilical artery may result from higher ACAN and VCAN expression and less proteolysis.

claim: Lower ACAN and VCAN expression and greater ADAMTS levels within the umbilical vein may preclude proteoglycan accumulation.

claim: Analysis of umbilical cords from nine large primate and non-primate mammals disclosed similar dimorphism as in humans.
source: Analysis of umbilical cords from nine large primate and non-primate mammals disclosed similar dimorphism, namely, umbilical arteries were occluded and had thicker walls with similar infolding of the inner arterial TM (Figure 3a) and strong Alcian blue and CS-staining, contrasting with veins (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Umbilical arteries in nine large mammalian species were occluded and had thicker walls with infolding of the inner arterial TM.
source: Analysis of umbilical cords from nine large primate and non-primate mammals disclosed similar dimorphism, namely, umbilical arteries were occluded and had thicker walls with similar infolding of the inner arterial TM (Figure 3a) and strong Alcian blue and CS-staining, contrasting with veins (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Anti-aggrecan and anti-NITEGE staining confirmed aggrecan abundance in the inner arterial TM and robust aggrecan cleavage in the outer TM of the artery and the TM of the vein in several animal species.
source: Anti-aggrecan and anti-NITEGE stained several animal species, confirming aggrecan abundance in the inner arterial TM and robust aggrecan cleavage resulting from ADAMTS protease activity in the outer TM of the artery and the TM of the vein (Figure 3c–d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Mouse umbilical cords demonstrated vascular dimorphism.
source: Mouse umbilical cords also demonstrated vascular dimorphism (Figure 4a), suggesting that genetically modified mice would provide mechanistic insights into proteoglycan dynamics and its impact.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by histological data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Aggrecan and versican immunofluorescence showed strong staining in the mouse umbilical artery inner TM and adventitia, with weaker staining in the veins.
source: Aggrecan and versican immunofluorescence showed strong staining in the mouse umbilical artery inner TM and adventitia, with weaker staining in the veins (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Acan and Vcan were strongly expressed in the umbilical arteries at early (E12.5) and late (E18.5) gestational stages.
source: Acan, Vcan and Adamts1,4,5,9 RNA-ISH at early (E12.5) and late (E18.5) gestational stages showed that Acan and Vcan were strongly expressed in the umbilical arteries (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-ISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Adamts1 was the most highly expressed proteoglycanase in the mouse umbilical vein just prior to parturition (E18.5).
source: Adamts1 was the most highly expressed proteoglycanase in the mouse umbilical vein just prior to parturition (E18.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), evidenced by strong β-gal staining in venous TM, adventitia and endothelium; the inner umbilical artery TM and endothelium of Adamts1lacZ/+ embryos lacked β-gal staining (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-ISH and β-gal staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and Figure 4c.

claim: The inner umbilical artery TM and endothelium of Adamts1lacZ/+ embryos lacked β-gal staining.
source: Adamts1 was the most highly expressed proteoglycanase in the mouse umbilical vein just prior to parturition (E18.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), evidenced by strong β-gal staining in venous TM, adventitia and endothelium; the inner umbilical artery TM and endothelium of Adamts1lacZ/+ embryos lacked β-gal staining (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by β-gal staining data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Adamts9 mutant embryos have short umbilical cords, abnormal umbilical artery development, and die by 14.5 days of gestation.
source: Although Adamts9 mutant embryos were previously observed to have short umbilical cords, abnormal umbilical artery development, and to die by 14.5 days of gestation (Nandadasa et al., 2015), umbilical cord development was not previously investigated in mutants of the two genes implicated here as potentially critical for umbilical cord vascular dimorphism, Acan and Adamts1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Adamts1-/- and Acan-/- embryos had significantly short umbilical cords at E18.5.
source: At E18.5, Acan-/- and Adamts1-/- mutants each had significantly short umbilical cords (Figure 4d) demonstrating their requirement for proper umbilical cord development.

claim: Acan and Adamts1 are required for proper umbilical cord development.
source: At E18.5, Acan-/- and Adamts1-/- mutants each had significantly short umbilical cords (Figure 4d) demonstrating their requirement for proper umbilical cord development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the mutant phenotypes.

claim: Umbilical cord histology showed thinner vascular walls in Acan-/- umbilical vessels.

claim: Umbilical cord histology showed thicker vascular walls in Adamts1-/- umbilical vessels.

claim: Circumferential SMC reorientation occurs around E13.5 in mouse umbilical vessels.
source: At earlier developmental stages (E12.5 to E14.5), lack of aggrecan did not affect either umbilical cord length or circumferential SMC reorientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–d), which occurs around E13.5 and is defective in Adamts9 mutants (Nandadasa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Circumferential SMC reorientation is defective in Adamts9 mutants.
source: At earlier developmental stages (E12.5 to E14.5), lack of aggrecan did not affect either umbilical cord length or circumferential SMC reorientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–d), which occurs around E13.5 and is defective in Adamts9 mutants (Nandadasa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Lack of aggrecan did not impair the survival of mouse embryos until parturition.

claim: Acan-/- embryos were observed at the expected Mendelian ratio at E18.5.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genotype ratio data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Acan and Adamts1 appear to be involved in umbilical vessel development from early gestation, but their functions manifest near parturition.
source: Thus, Acan and Adamts1 appear to be involved in umbilical vessel development from early gestation, but their functions manifest near parturition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the developmental timing of mutant phenotypes.

claim: The arterial and venous lumina were smaller in Adamts1-/- mice relative to wild-type.
source: The arterial and venous lumina were smaller in Adamts1-/- mice relative to wild-type, indicating that their thicker vascular walls compromised luminal diameter, and larger in Acan-/- mice (Figure 4e–g).

claim: The arterial and venous lumina were larger in Acan-/- mice relative to wild-type.
source: The arterial and venous lumina were smaller in Adamts1-/- mice relative to wild-type, indicating that their thicker vascular walls compromised luminal diameter, and larger in Acan-/- mice (Figure 4e–g).

claim: Thicker vascular walls in Adamts1-/- mice compromised luminal diameter.
